_readme: Passenger prose, as data rather than code. Add lines freely - every pool
is independent and the paragraph is assembled one slot at a time, so a
new line cannot break another. Keep the voice: a passenger in the back,
wry, observant, describing what they felt rather than what the
instruments said. American spelling.
Placeholders: openings take {aircraft}, {duration_adj} ('18-minute') and
{duration_noun} ('18 minutes'). Landing lines take {rate} ('91 fpm').
Nothing else is substituted, and an unknown placeholder is left alone.
'held' is the pool for a landing whose letter was pulled down by how it
arrived rather than how hard: gentle on the wheels, then crooked or
sliding. Those lines must not call the touchdown firm, because it wasn't.
'connector' is a short bridging sentence, used only when the ride and the
landing pull in opposite directions - 'up' when the landing rescued a bad
ride, 'down' when it spoiled a good one. Without it the paragraph reads
as two unrelated verdicts stapled together. Keep them SHORT.
closer 'mixed' is for exactly that case. A leg whose parts disagree must
not end on 'well flown, start to finish' - it wasn't.
closer 'mixed' lines must work in BOTH directions - the good half may
have been the ride or the landing. 'One good landing does not make a
good flight' was in here and read as praise for a 509 fpm arrival.
